claims.text: Premelting and melting behavior of high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles is primarily governed by size-dependent surface-energy effects.
Smaller nanoparticles have a larger surface-to-volume ratio.
A larger surface-to-volume ratio increases the relative contribution of surface free energy.
The increased contribution of surface free energy lowers the effective melting point and initiates premelting at lower temperatures.
Compositionally uniform HEA nanoparticles can be synthesized with controlled composition and defect density.
Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi is a suitable example of the controlled HEA nanoparticle system.
Nanoparticle size can be varied through synthesis parameters such as precursor concentration and flame temperature in flame spray pyrolysis while holding composition constant.
HEA nanoparticle batches with narrow mean-diameter distributions spanning 5–50 nm can be prepared under otherwise identical conditions.
In situ high-resolution TEM can monitor thermally induced nanoscale structural changes in real time.
DSC, high-resolution TEM, and differential electron microscopy can jointly determine premelting and melting onset in these HEA nanoparticles.
Increasing the proportion of surface atoms destabilizes the lattice.
Increasing the proportion of surface atoms reduces the energy barrier for atomic mobility.
Smaller HEA nanoparticles will premelt and melt at lower temperatures than larger nanoparticles of the same composition.
Melting onset will shift continuously with particle size throughout the 5–50 nm diameter range.
The proposed size dependence should hold from 5 nm to 50 nm when composition is uniform and defect and polydispersity effects are minimal.
Compositional fluctuations, residual defects, size-distribution variability, and in situ measurement artifacts can confound the observed size dependence.
Failure to observe a statistically significant association between decreasing particle size and depressed premelting or melting onset would falsify the proposed size-dependent mechanism.
